pack.title: Comparing the operation counts of catalogue routines

provenance.notes: Constants and the three routine names are invented for this pack so that every question turns on the supplied figures rather than on remembered complexity results.

repairs.reason: Three questions carried narrowing leaks, two of them caused by q3 alone. q3 was a special case of q6 — both turned on the rankings reshuffling across the tabulated sizes — and its options enumerated Table 1’s three column headings, which confirmed for q1 that n = 16 is a literal table row. Separately, q7’s answer was a clean multiple of the catalogue size, so dividing its options by 4,096 left two candidate SPLIT values that q2’s option cluster then separated on magnitude.

changed.gam-cs-oc-001-q2: Unchanged in the end. A distractor swap (315 for 340, Table 1’s SPLIT count at n = 4096) was drafted and withdrawn: naming 340 in an option hands q7 a value it must take from the table, and the mechanical gate rejected it as sibling-option leakage. Recorded here because the withdrawal is part of the repair, not an absence of one.
changed.gam-cs-oc-001-q3: Replaced. Was "at which listed size does SPLIT perform more steps than SCAN"; is now a sensitivity question on SPLIT’s own count across two doublings. It ranks no routines against one another, names no catalogue size, and — after the mechanical gate caught a first draft that named the formula’s two constants in its options, which would have handed them to q2 — carries no numbers at all.
changed.gam-cs-oc-001-q7: Revised. The artificial "ignoring SCAN’s own steps" clause is dropped and the question asks for the program’s total, which exercises both of the text’s composition rules rather than one. No option is now a clean multiple of the catalogue size.

repairs.unchanged: q1, q4, q5 and q6 keep their content; q1 and q6 were leak targets, not leak sources.

provenance.retiredBecause: Fails spec §5.9 at pack level. The independent round of 8 September 2026 — Claude Opus 5 on both halves, neither shown the answer key — rated six of the pack’s seven questions DECISIVELY coupled, and demonstrated the mechanism: the option lists reconstruct Table 1 in full without the table being seen. q7’s options factor exactly into SPLIT(4096) = 340 and SCAN(4096) = 16,414; q2’s options are spaced by exactly 25 and q3 asserts a constant rise per doubling, giving SPLIT(n) = 40 + 25 log2 n; q5’s first option is SCAN(256), giving SCAN(n) = 4n + 30; q1’s 128 and 32,768 stand in the ratio of one table step squared, giving PAIR(n) = n^2 / 2. Every row of the table follows, and with it six of the seven answers. No key is wrong — both rounds agreed with all seven — and there is no ambiguity, outside-knowledge or §5.10 finding against it. The fault is the arithmetic relationship between the option lists, which is a pack-level design fault: each item is individually sound. Retiring the six coupled questions would leave one, so this is retirement under its proper name. A replacement should carry at most two numeric items on one table, or use a source whose questions do not all reduce to arithmetic on the same few constants. Kept in full as the evidence; counts for nothing.
provenance.retirementCaveat: ADJUDICATOR STRENGTH DECIDED THIS. The same seven questions were adjudicated one day earlier by Claude Sonnet 5, which rated three of them narrowing and NONE decisive. Nothing about the content changed between the two rounds. The pack was re-run under the stronger reader only because the step-rebate pack had been, and comparing packs judged by different readers would have been meaningless. Had that re-run not happened, this pack would have been reported as the mildest of the four. That is the strongest evidence this pilot has produced that a clean adjudication round describes the reader as much as the content.

blocks.text: Comparing the operation counts of catalogue routines

The operation count of a routine, written T(n), is the number of elementary steps it carries out on an input of n records. An elementary step is a single comparison, assignment or arithmetic operation. Two routines can grow at the same rate and still differ by a large constant factor, and at the input sizes a program actually meets, that constant is often what decides which routine finishes first.

Three routines are compared here, all of which search a catalogue of records. SCAN examines every record once. SPLIT repeatedly halves the range still under consideration. PAIR compares every record with every other record. Their operation counts on a catalogue of n records are given below.

blocks.caption: Operation counts of the three routines on a catalogue of n records.

legend.meaning: number of records in the catalogue

blocks.caption: Operation counts of the three routines at three catalogue sizes.

blocks.text: When two routines run one after the other on the same catalogue, their operation counts are added. When one routine is run once for every record that another routine processes, the inner routine’s count is multiplied by the number of records processed, and not by the outer routine’s own count.

A routine is only worth replacing if the replacement performs fewer steps at the catalogue sizes that actually occur. Below a certain size a routine whose count grows faster may still perform fewer steps than one whose count grows more slowly, because the slower-growing routine begins with a larger fixed cost.

questions.stem: According to Table 1, how many elementary steps does PAIR perform on a catalogue of 16 records?
questions.explanation: Table 1 lists the operation counts of each routine at three catalogue sizes. Reading along the PAIR row to the n = 16 column gives 128 elementary steps.

a.reason: 94 is SCAN's count at n = 16 — the right column but the wrong row.

c.reason: 140 is SPLIT's count at n = 16 — again the right column and the wrong row.

d.reason: 32768 is PAIR's count at n = 256, one column too far to the right.

hints.text: Everything you need is in the table; no calculation is required.
Find the row for the routine named in the question, then the column for the catalogue size named in the question.
Read across the PAIR row until you reach the column headed n = 16.

questions.stem: A catalogue holds 1,024 records. How many elementary steps does SPLIT perform on it?
questions.explanation: 1,024 is 2 multiplied by itself ten times, so its logarithm to base 2 is 10. SPLIT’s count is 25 × 10 + 40 = 290 elementary steps. The catalogue size is not one of the three in Table 1, so the count has to come from the formula.

a.reason: 265 uses 9 for the logarithm, which is the value for 512 records rather than 1,024. Doubling the catalogue adds one to the logarithm.

c.reason: 315 uses 11 for the logarithm, which is the value for 2,048 records. 1,024 is 2 multiplied by itself ten times, not eleven.

d.reason: 1,064 adds the fixed cost of 40 to the number of records themselves. It is the logarithm of the number of records that is multiplied by 25, not the number of records.

hints.text: The catalogue size is not one of the three in Table 1, so the table cannot answer this.
Ask how many times 1,024 can be halved before one record is left.
Put that count into SPLIT’s formula in place of the logarithm, then add the fixed cost.

questions.stem: A catalogue is doubled in size, and then doubled again. According to the counts given, how does the number of elementary steps SPLIT performs change across the two doublings?

options.text: It rises by the same number of steps at each doubling.
It rises by more steps at the second doubling than at the first.
It rises by fewer steps at the second doubling than at the first.
It quadruples, as the catalogue does.

questions.explanation: Doubling a number adds one to its logarithm to base 2, because one further halving is now needed to reach a single record. SPLIT’s count is that logarithm multiplied by a fixed coefficient, plus a fixed cost that never moves. Each doubling therefore adds one lot of the coefficient and nothing else, so the two doublings cost the same as one another however large the catalogue was to begin with.

b.reason: A rise that grows with each doubling belongs to a count proportional to the number of records, or to its square. SPLIT’s count follows the logarithm, and a doubling adds one to a logarithm wherever it starts from.

c.reason: The rise does not shrink either. The logarithm gains exactly one at every doubling, so the count gains exactly one lot of its coefficient at every doubling.

d.reason: A count that quadruples when the catalogue quadruples is proportional to the number of records. SPLIT does not examine the records one by one — it halves the range still under consideration, and its count follows the logarithm rather than the number itself.

hints.text: Only one of the two terms in SPLIT’s count can move when the catalogue size moves.
Ask what doubling a number does to its logarithm to base 2, and then what doubling it again does.
Compare the two rises with each other rather than working either of them out.

questions.stem: A catalogue grows from 4,096 records to 8,192 records. By approximately what factor does PAIR's operation count change?
questions.explanation: PAIR's count is n squared divided by two. Doubling n multiplies n squared by four, and the division by two is unchanged, so the count is multiplied by about four.

a.reason: PAIR's count depends on n, so it cannot stay the same when n changes.

b.reason: Doubling would follow if the count were proportional to n, which is SCAN's rule rather than PAIR's.

d.reason: The count rises with n, so a larger catalogue cannot reduce it.

hints.text: You do not need the table for this — only the rule that governs PAIR.
Look at how n enters PAIR's expression, and ask what happens to that term when n is doubled.
Write the count for the new size as a multiple of the count for the old size and cancel the common divisor.

questions.stem: A program runs SPLIT once and then runs SCAN once, both on the same catalogue of 256 records. Using the values in Table 1, how many elementary steps does the program perform in total?

supportSpans.quote: When two routines run one after the other on the same catalogue, their operation counts are added.

questions.explanation: The two routines run one after the other, so their counts are added. Table 1 gives SPLIT 240 steps and SCAN 1054 steps at n = 256, and 240 + 1054 = 1294.

a.reason: 1054 counts only SCAN and ignores the SPLIT run that precedes it.

c.reason: 1314 adds SPLIT's count at n = 4096 (340) instead of its count at n = 256.

d.reason: 252,960 multiplies the two counts, which the text reserves for the case where one routine runs once per record processed by another.

hints.text: The text states how counts combine in two different situations. Decide which one this is.
The two routines run in sequence on the same catalogue, not one inside the other.
Take both counts from the n = 256 column and combine them in the way the text prescribes for routines run one after the other.

questions.stem: Which statement holds across all three catalogue sizes listed in Table 1?

options.text: PAIR performs the most elementary steps at every listed size.
SCAN performs more elementary steps than PAIR at every listed size.
No single routine performs the fewest elementary steps at every listed size.
PAIR performs the fewest elementary steps at the smallest listed size.

supportSpans.quote: Below a certain size a routine whose count grows faster may still perform fewer steps than one whose count grows more slowly

questions.explanation: The routine with the fewest steps changes as the catalogue grows: at the smallest size it is SCAN, and at both larger sizes it is SPLIT. That is the situation the text describes, where a faster-growing count can still be the smaller one below a certain size.

a.reason: PAIR does take the most steps at the two larger sizes, but not at the smallest, where SPLIT's 140 exceeds its 128.

b.reason: The comparison runs the other way at every listed size: SCAN takes fewer steps than PAIR at all three, not more.

d.reason: At the smallest size SCAN takes 94 steps against PAIR's 128, so PAIR is not the fewest there.

hints.text: Test each statement against all three columns; one column is enough to defeat a claim.
The smallest catalogue size behaves differently from the other two.
Ask which routine has the smallest entry in each column, and whether it is the same routine each time.

questions.stem: A program processes a catalogue of 4,096 records with SCAN, and for every record that SCAN examines it runs SPLIT once over the whole catalogue. How many elementary steps does the program perform in total?

supportSpans.quote: the inner routine’s count is multiplied by the number of records processed, and not by the outer routine’s own count

questions.explanation: Table 1 gives SCAN 16,414 steps and SPLIT 340 steps at n = 4096. SCAN examines each of the 4,096 records once, and each examination triggers one full run of SPLIT, so the SPLIT runs contribute 4,096 × 340 = 1,392,640 steps. SCAN’s own 16,414 steps are performed as well, giving 1,409,054 in total.

a.reason: Adding SCAN’s 16,414 to SPLIT’s 340 is the count for running the two routines one after the other. Here one runs inside the other, so SPLIT’s count multiplies before anything is added.

b.reason: This is the contribution of the SPLIT runs alone. SCAN performs its own steps while it examines the records, and the question asks what the program performs in total.

d.reason: This multiplies SPLIT’s count by SCAN’s own count, which is the reading the text rules out. What multiplies SPLIT’s count is the number of records processed, not the number of steps SCAN takes to process them.

hints.text: Decide first whether the two counts should be added or multiplied, and find the sentence that settles it.
One SPLIT run happens for each record SCAN examines, and SCAN examines every record once.
The question asks what the program performs altogether, so SCAN’s own work belongs in the answer too.
